bmt-2016-team-01.title: Cosine doubling
bmt-2016-team-01.body:
Write $a_1=2\cos\frac\pi6$. Since $(2\cos\theta)^2-2=2\cos2\theta$, $a_n=2\cos\left(2^{n-1}\frac\pi6\right)$. So $a_{2016}=2\cos\left(\frac{2^{2014}\pi}{3}\right)$. Now $2^{2014}\equiv4\pmod6$ ($2^{2k}\equiv4\pmod 6$ for $k\ge1$), so the angle is $\equiv\frac{4\pi}{3}\pmod{2\pi}$ and the value is $2\cdot(-\tfrac12)=-1$.

**Answer: $-1$**

bmt-2016-team-02.title: Corner triangles
bmt-2016-team-02.body:
Cut isosceles right triangles with legs $x$; the octagon side is the hypotenuse $x\sqrt2$ and also the remaining part of the square side: $1-2x$. So $x\sqrt2=1-2x$, $x=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt2}$, side $=x\sqrt2=\frac{\sqrt2}{2+\sqrt2}=\sqrt2-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2-1$**

bmt-2016-team-03.title: Two trips for one loop
bmt-2016-team-03.body:
The center line of the strip has length $12$ inches. Because of the half twist, after traveling once around the center line the train is back at the same place on the strip but flipped to the other side of the paper; it returns to its starting point (same point, same side) only after going around twice, $24$ inches, i.e. $2$ minutes. Two complete loops take $4$ minutes.

**Answer: 4 minutes**

bmt-2016-team-04.title: Impossible
bmt-2016-team-04.body:
The vertex of degree $5$ is adjacent to all other vertices. Hence the two vertices of degree $1$ have no other neighbors. The vertex of degree $4$ is then adjacent to the degree-$5$ vertex and can only use the vertices of degrees $2$ and $3$ besides, so it has at most $3$ neighbors, a contradiction. No such graph exists.

**Answer: 0**

bmt-2016-team-06.title: Square-factor count
bmt-2016-team-06.body:
If $n=\prod p^{e_p}$ the number of square divisors is $\prod(\lfloor e_p/2\rfloor+1)$. This equals $3$ iff one prime has $e_p\in\{4,5\}$ and every other prime has $e\le1$. So $n=p^4m$ or $p^5m$ with $m$ squarefree and coprime to $p$. Below $400$: $p=2$: $16m$ with $m$ odd squarefree $<25$: $11$ values; $32m$, $m<12.5$ odd squarefree: $1,3,5,7,11$: $5$ values; $p=3$: $81m$, $m\in\{1,2\}$: $2$ values, and $243$: $1$ value; $p\ge5$: $625>400$. Total $11+5+2+1=19$.

**Answer: 19**

bmt-2016-team-07.title: Bilinear form
bmt-2016-team-07.body:
The first condition says that for each fixed $x$, $f(x,\cdot)$ is an arithmetic progression (linear in $y$); the second says that for each fixed $y$, $f(\cdot,y)$ is linear in $x$. So $f(x,y)=a+bx+cy+dxy$ (determined by $f(0,0),f(1,0),f(0,1),f(1,1)$: for each fixed $x$, linear in $y$ with coefficients linear in $x$). Conversely every such function works. There are $4$ free parameters, and the values at $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$ determine them, while fewer than $4$ values cannot determine $4$ parameters.

**Answer: 4**

bmt-2016-team-08.title: Stars and bars
bmt-2016-team-08.body:
Give each Berkeley student one candy first. The remaining $7$ candies are distributed among $7$ students with no restrictions: $\binom{7+7-1}{7-1}=\binom{13}{6}=1716$.

**Answer: 1716**

bmt-2016-team-09.title: Recurrence
bmt-2016-team-09.body:
Let $c_n$ count subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with no three consecutive integers. Looking at the first omitted element among $1,2,3$ (or none): $c_n=c_{n-1}+c_{n-2}+c_{n-3}$ for $n\ge3$, with $c_0=1$, $c_1=2$, $c_2=4$. So $c_3=7$, $c_4=13$, $c_5=24$, $c_6=44$.

**Answer: 44**

bmt-2016-team-10.title: Search over short vectors
bmt-2016-team-10.body:
Translate so one vertex is the origin; the other vertices are lattice vectors $u,v$ with $|\det(u,v)|=1$ (area $\frac12$), and no side is axis-parallel means $u$, $v$, $u-v$ have both coordinates nonzero. The shortest such vectors have lengths $\sqrt2$ (like $(1,1)$), $\sqrt5$ (like $(1,2)$), then $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{13}$ (like $(2,3)$); vectors like $(2,2)$ cannot occur as a side of an area-$\frac12$ triangle. Checking all small combinations, the smallest perimeter is attained by $u=(1,1)$, $v=(2,3)$, $v-u=(1,2)$ with $\det=1$, giving sides $\sqrt2,\sqrt5,\sqrt{13}$, for example the triangle $(-3,-3),(-2,-2),(-1,0)$. A computer search over all such triangles confirms nothing has smaller perimeter.

**Answer: $\sqrt2+\sqrt5+\sqrt{13}$**

bmt-2016-team-11.title: Radical axis
bmt-2016-team-11.body:
$D$ lies on the radical axis $XY$, so its powers with respect to the two circles are equal: $DA^2$ (tangent to $C_1$ at $A$) $=DB\cdot DC$. Put $AB=1$, $BC=2016$ on a line with $A=0,B=1,C=2017$ and $D=d$: $d^2=(d-1)(d-2017)$, so $d=\frac{2017}{2018}$ and $BD=1-d=\frac1{2018}$. Then $1+\frac{BC}{BD}=1+2016\cdot2018=2017^2$, and the answer is $2017$ (the radii are not needed).

**Answer: 2017**

bmt-2016-team-12.title: Integrate slices
bmt-2016-team-12.body:
Slices at height $z$ are disks of area $\pi(1-z^2)$. The volume is $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\int_0^1z\pi(1-z^2)\,dz=\pi\left(\frac12-\frac14\right)=\frac\pi4$. So $\bar z=\frac{\pi/4}{2\pi/3}=\frac38$.

**Answer: $\frac38$**

bmt-2016-team-13.title: Wald / linearity
bmt-2016-team-13.body:
Each black ball takes on average $\frac{101}{50}$ turns (geometric with success probability $\frac{50}{101}$). For a given $n$ the expected number of turns is $\frac{101n}{50}$. Averaging over $n$, $E[n]=\frac{101}{2}$, so the answer is $\frac{101}{50}\cdot\frac{101}{2}=\frac{10201}{100}=102.01$.

**Answer: $\frac{10201}{100}$**

bmt-2016-team-14.title: VC dimension of boxes
bmt-2016-team-14.body:
$n\ge2d$: take the $2d$ points $\pm e_i$. For a subset $P$, let the $i$th interval of the box be $[a_i,b_i]$ with $b_i=1$ if $e_i\in P$ else $\frac12$, and $a_i=-1$ if $-e_i\in P$ else $-\frac12$. Each interval contains $0$, so a point $\pm e_j$ lies in the box iff its $j$th coordinate $\pm1$ lies in $[a_j,b_j]$, i.e. iff it is in $P$.

$n\le2d$: given $2d+1$ points, in each coordinate mark the points with the smallest and the largest value there; at most $2d$ points are marked, so some point $z$ is unmarked. Let $P$ be all points except $z$. Any box containing $P$ contains, in each coordinate, the min and max values, hence contains $z$ too. So $S$ cannot be shattered.

**Answer: $2d$**

bmt-2016-team-15.title: Sophie Germain factorization
bmt-2016-team-15.body:
$4s^4+81=(2s^2+9)^2-36s^2=(2s^2+6s+9)(2s^2-6s+9)$. Write $2s^2+6s+9=2(s-\alpha)(s-\bar\alpha)$ with $\alpha=\frac{-3+3i}{2}$, and $2s^2-6s+9=2(s+\alpha)(s+\bar\alpha)$. With $p(x)=x^3+x^2+\frac92x+9=\prod(x-s_i)$ we have $\prod_i(s_i-\alpha)=-p(\alpha)$, so the product is $2^6\,|p(\alpha)|^2|p(-\alpha)|^2$ (sign: $(-1)^{12}=1$).

Compute: $\alpha^2=-\frac{9i}{2}$, $\alpha^3=\frac{27+27i}{4}$, so $p(\alpha)=9+9i$, $|p(\alpha)|^2=162$; $p(-\alpha)=9-18i$, $|p(-\alpha)|^2=405$. The product is $64\cdot162\cdot405=2^7\cdot3^8\cdot5$, so $a+b+c=7+8+1=16$.

**Answer: 16**
